or about what needs to be done. But we will see what happens there and times will be
interesting.
I will say, though, that the people of Northland at first were a little bit— I have got to
say, you know, Winston was there in the bus and they kind of stopped and took stock
for a moment and were not quite expecting him. But they really have got a bit sick of
being talked down to. So at first they did sort of go—they are a bit sick of him. And did
you notice that the members’ debate was all about how awful Northland is, how awfully
things are going, how terrible things are, and how bad it is—you know, it is so bad up in
Northland. I actually think that it is one of the most incredible regions in this country, as
it has more going for it than most of them do and it is pretty damned incredible. S o does
our candidate, Mark Osborne, and that is what National stands for. So the little rhetoric
of talking them down and saying how bad things are, you know, might have initially got
a bit of TV coverage, but the people of Northland, they know how great t he place that
they live in is, they know how great they are, and they do not believe in the negativity
from New Zealand First, which, quite frankly, they are hearing all the time.
So Labour really is in a bit of disarray over here. Here those members are, sort of
struggling along, and then the person whom they have got to look at as their great
shining light is Winston Peters. So they throw their own candidate, Willow -Jean Prime,
under the Winston Peters bus. She is actually quite an awesome woman, from some
accounts up north, I have got to say. There is quite a bit of respect for her there and they
think that she is actually a strong candidate who could do a really good job—those, of
course, who do not support our wonderful candidate, Mark Osborne. But under the bus
she goes, not even overtly, but covertly. So they have not got the actual chutzpah to
stand up and actually say: “This is what we believe, but we will all secretly hope that
Winston is our great saviour up there because things are not going so w ell for Labour
itself.”
So let us take the housing policy. Obviously the member Phil Twyford is getting
ready for his great debate. He is ready to get up there and give it stick. Those members
do not know where they stand on housing. So it is State housing that Labour largely
ignored—build a couple more houses and the job is done. It does not matter that they
are in the wrong place with the wrong people and are not actually addressing the needs
of tenants. That is pretty much like: “Just tick that box and we have done our housing
policy, and everything is all right.” The member blatantly gets up and in speeches says
that he supports growing community housing providers. He says private sector
investment is part of that—local government and central government . He blatantly says
it all of the time. He makes up, quite frankly, real stories and untruths about this
2584 General Debate 25 Mar 2015
Government trying to flog heaps off to private developers, which I right now put on the
record as saying is untrue. It is point-blank untrue.
What we stand for are tenants. What we stand for, and will make a difference on, is
actually people who have been left behind, largely ignored for generations, and who
now deserve to have the right kinds of services wrapped around them by the right kind
of community providers. That takes leadership. It means standing up for something and
backing those providers with the right level of funding and the right level of support
around them. That is what we stand for and that is what we believe in.

items.speaker: PHIL TWYFORD
items.text: The last few weeks have been very, very
revealing. What the Northland by -election has exposed is a classically arrogant third -
term National Government that is mired in scandal, is desperate to hold on to power,
and is frantically trying to cover up its ow n shortcomings—in this particular instance,
the Northland by -election and its chronic neglect of regional New Zealand over many,
many years. It has basically been like watching a slow -motion train wreck. I do not
know what will be the most enduring image of the campaign. On the one hand it might
be Simon Bridges, Steven Joyce, the hapless Mark Osborne, and a large black pig trying
to erect a National Party hoarding —a photograph that appeared on the front page of the
Northern Advocate—and on the other hand, it might be the poor candidate Mark
Osborne, who had been advised not to go into the studio for the Q+A interview, with his
eyes darting nervously from side to side and Steven Joyce clearly there behind the
camera holding up cue cards telling him what to say.
So what did National do? It panicked. It panicked after one media opinion poll
showed it was likely to lose this by -election. Steven Joyce panicked and he threw $70
million of taxpayers’ money at 10 Northland bridges that the Northland Regional
Council had not even been asking for in its regional transport plan. In fact, only three of
the 10 bridges were even mentioned, and of those three, only two of them got the lowest
possible priority rating. They were not a priority for Northland. But this National
Government has never seen a political problem that could not be solved by throwing
truckloads of taxpayers’ money at it. And for this Minister of Transport, Simon Bridges,
his reputation has been one of the great casualties of this by -election campaign because
he will never ever have any financial credibility or credibility as a transport Minister in
this Parliament again. Simon Bridges’ bridges —his reputation has been permanently
tarnished. The hapless candidate Mark Osborne could not even name the bridge s, even
though he can see one of them from his front window. He claims it was his idea to think
of the bridges in the first place, and yet he could not even name them.
Matthew Hooton, who is not exactly a firebrand socialist, has said that the pork-
barrel politics practised by this National Government are the worst since the National
Government of Sir Robert Muldoon in the 1970s and 1980s. This is the by -election of
pork, and it will hang around the necks of Steven Joyce, Simon Bridges, and all the
other maestros who have been involved in running the campaign. I have a question: is
the pork- barrel politics a sign of how desperate and how panicky this National
Government is about losing the by -election this Saturday, or is it an indicator of how
casual the Go vernment is with taxpayers’ money and of how willing it is to spend it
willy-nilly in the pursuit of power and in buying votes? Or is it both of those things? I
suggest it is the third.
Not only have we seen bribery but we have also seen bullying. And poor  Shane Reti,
who was sent out by Steven Joyce and Simon Bridges to tell the people of Pipiwai in
Northland who are simply campaigning to get their dusty roads sealed —a reasonable
enough request—he was sent there to bully and intimidate the people of Pipiwai. It is all
over the media. He was sent there to tell them that they should keep quiet and that they
should keep their heads down for the duration of this by -election, otherwise they would
25 Mar 2015 General Debate 2585
get nothing. That is the National Party in this by -election—bullying, intimidation, pork-
barrel politics. He told the people of Pipiwai that he had taken their roads plan to
Cabinet, and he was forced to retract that statement. The Minister exposed that for the
lie that it is.
It is not the pork. It is not the years of neglect. It is not the dusty roads, the blackmail,
the bullying, and the lying. The thing that really sticks in the craw of the people of
Northland is that they were kept in the dark by this National Party about Mike Sabin
and the police investigation.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member knows that that is not a subject that will be
raised in this House.

items.speaker: PHIL TWYFORD
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I want to point out, in
relation to that, that 3 News published—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I do not care what 3 News  has done. I have made it quite
clear, and the Standing Orders are quite clear, that that matter will not be discussed in
this House. That concludes the member’s speech, anyway.

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: After years of neglect by the
left, when Winston Peters was off traipsing around the world and Phil Goff was funding
hip-hop tours in Auckland, we are back backing the regions. Ron Mark wants to talk
about bridges in Northland. They are certainly topical. I really like Bridges. I like them
so much I have made two small ones of my own. I probably will not make 10; we will
see how it goes.
Through the life of this Government we have spent hundreds of millions —actually,
billions—of dollars more than the left building roads and bridges in regional New
Zealand.

items.speaker: Ron Mark
items.text: Cutting rural road funding.

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: We know, Ron Mark, unlike the left, that right at this
moment, because it is convenient to Ron Mark, his party, “Winston First”, is sidling up
to—we know that the way it does roads is that only two or three cities in New Zealand
get a look-in. Well, it is not what this Government has done. We have supplemented the
regions of this country and made sure they get the good Government investments they
deserve. They do not see those investments as —to use the words we have heard—pork
barrel politics. They see th em as quality investments that are essential lifelines to their
people.
We have been backing the regions. We have done that through the National Land
Transport Fund. We have put much more into that, really, across all of the categories.
We have made sure there are categories in it that appropriately recognise the role of the
regions because we know that under the way that Labour used to do things, they did not
get a fair go.
Ron Mark says we have cut funding. Well, let me give Ron Mark a few little
statistics here in relation to what was spent in 2005 to 2008 and what is being spent in
2012 to 2015 in some of the regions in this country. Basically, almost every single
region has gone up, most of them significantly. The Bay of Plenty is up 47 percent ,
from $322 million to $475 million in the National Land Transport Fund. Canterbury is
up 200 percent , to $1 billion. Hawke’s Bay is up 18 percent , to $188 million.
Marlborough, Nelson, and Tasman are up 47 percent. Otago is up 36 percent. Southland
is up 35 percent. Taranaki is up 41 percent. Waikato is up 50 percent. The West Coast is
up 23 percent. We have spent more in the regions because we know they are an
important part of this country. We have been backing them.
That backing has not just been through the National Land Transport Programme. It
has not just been in other conventional ways. We have also recognised and accepted that
sometimes projects that the regions really back and that are vital to those areas need us
2586 General Debate 25 Mar 2015
to come in and make an assessment of what is required. That is why we have done that
in the Accelerated Regional Roading Package. That is why in that package we have
systematically gone through and chosen many projects all over New Zealand. There  is
the Kawarau Gorge bridge in Otago, which I kno w that the member of Parliament there
is really excited about.  We keep going with bridges, whether they are the Normanby
Overbridge realignment in Taranaki, where I was privileged to turn the first sod very
recently—my first go in a digger—the bridges in Manawatū and Whanganui; or the one
that I know that Anne Tolley has been banging on about for probably far too long. This
Government—because the last Government would not do anything, despite the fact that
it had been a regional priority —is going to do some thing about the Motu Bridge
replacement in Gisborne. It is going to see it double -laned and improved because this is
the party, on this side of the House, that backs the regions.
I say to the members opposite that it is all very well to do Winston and do the hooey;
we do the “do-ey”, actually. We are the ones, on this side of the House, who for the last
several years, year on year , no matter what metric you choose, have spent more in the
regions than the left when Winston was propping it up—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Refer to members properly.

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: I have got a little friendly advice for the members
opposite. If they want to do well in the regions and they want to back the regions, they
could start by actually just supporting the conventional things we do. The member
opposite knows this. He knows that the Pūhoi to Wellsford approach is a good one. We
do not call it a “Holiday Highway” on this side of the House. We back the regions
throughout this country, and we are going to continue to do so.

items.speaker: STEFFAN BROWNING
items.text: Yesterday an international research study was
published by the American Society for Microbiology on its open access journal mBio .
The significance of this report is that it found that some herbicides in common garden
use, in common agricultural use, and often in pesticide food residues may undermine
antibiotic therapy and increase levels of antibiotic resistance in some disease- causing
bacteria. One of the herbicides was Monsanto’s glyphosate -based Roundup, and it is
familiar to most New Zealanders, including those over here. That is right —the
ubiquitous Roundup, the Roundup in many garden sheds, and on most farms, and many,
many vi neyards has once again been seriously implicated with effects that could be
seriously affecting our children’s health, our health, and that of animals and even bees.
But this study is not on its own. Just 5 days ago we heard that the International
Agency for Research on Cancer has identified glyphosate, the principal ingredient in
Roundup, as a probable carcinogen. We need to take this exceptionally seriously. There
are numerous other reports that show evidence is mounting that there are health risks
associated with Roundup, from babies to bees, yet we are not seeing evidence that this
Government is taking these real risks seriously. There are residues, including those in
Roundup or its breakdown chemicals, in many of the foods we eat and Roundup is
widely used on people’s backyards, driveways, footpaths, roads, and, increasingly,
whole paddocks and hillsides. We know that the folklore about drinking Roundup is
absolutely dangerous rubbish. Roundup is increasingly seen as dangerous, right up to
the United Na tions. It is a probable carcinogen and now linked to antibiotic resistance.
Those are just this week’s entries on the list. There are many more effects, including
birth defects and very concerning effects on the environment, including on bees and on
the soil biology of our productive lands.
Considering the evidence of pesticides affecting human health, typically we find that
the Ministry for Primary Industries’ total diet survey is done something like every 5
years. It is only a relatively small sample of foods as well —so when will this
Government increase monitoring of foods and residues? Unfortunately, the Ministry for
25 Mar 2015 General Debate 2587
Primary Industries spins the results of those residue tests and it quotes many, many
compounds in multi -residue tests that are not even relevant. It does that to statistically
inflate its testing effort, but it plays down the fact that most fruit and vegetables and
imported corn and soy products will have some pesticide residues in them. That is
right—most of the foods have some pesticide residues in them.
So when will this Government get stuck in and address the fact that consumers want
no pesticides in their food? They want no carcinogenic ones, none that increase
antibiotic resistance, none that are endocrine disruptors, no neurotoxins —they want
none. When will this Government get pesticides like Roundup out of New Zealanders’
food? Almost all the 600 Ministry for Primary Industries samples analysed in the Safe
Food Campaign’s dirty dozen list contained pesticide residues. They are impacti ng on
human health, even at low residue levels, and the Government needs to lift its game to
get pesticides out of New Zealand’s food.
Other studies are much more direct. Among New Zealanders, I am sick of hearing of
friends being taken to the hospice —including one of mine today —and hearing of
friends and family dying or suffering from cancers, significant allergies, and ongoing
health issues. We all have friends in that situation. It does not have to be that way, and it
was not, once. When will this Gover nment care about our babies and the bees and stop
relying on single-ingredient chemical safety tests, when we know that the chemicals in
each of the compounds also have adjuvants that are not being considered by our food
safety experts and that have been s hown to increase toxicity by up to a thousandfold?
Roundup is far more than its principal ingredient, glyphosate. Let us test food—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member’s time has expired.

items.speaker: Hon CRAIG FOSS
items.text: In just 1 month from today we
will be commemorating 100 years since the New Zealand Anzac troops came ashore at
Gallipoli. In just 1 month today it will be the centenary. As everyone in this House
knows, the Gallipoli centenary is a hugely significant event not only for New Zealand
and for our good Australian mates but, of course, for our friends in Turkey as we all
commemorate, evaluate, and have another look at the conflict of 1915.
I will be attending the Gallipoli commemorations along with our Prime Minister and
2,000 other New Zealanders. I actually was there about 2 months ago and I can
categorically state that it is a very special, personal experience and place for any New
Zealander—and I am sure for any Australian and Turkish person as well. It is an
extremely special place for understanding who we are as a country, why we are the
people we are, and why we have this great relationship with our friends the Aussies. We
can give them a hard time, but when push comes to shove, we stand side by side with
them in times of conflict and when necessary. The building of, the learning about, and
the beginning of our nationhood—about just what it means to be a Kiwi—that comes
through louder ever y year as we see more people, more younger New Zealanders, at
Anzac commemorations around our country. I personally think that as well as
respectfully looking at the sacrifice made by so many New Zealanders at the time, many
of whom were about the same age  as many of the schoolkids who go to these
commemorations are, it is perhaps a bit of a search as to who we are as a nation and
what formed us.
I have had the absolute pleasure today of hosting Ahmet Cinar, the Governor of
Turkey’s Çanakkale Province, who is currently visiting New Zealand. I spoke and met
with the Governor as he hosted me in Çanakkale, Gallipoli, a couple of months ago, and
I can assure you that we have friends in Gallipoli looking out for and looking after and
treasuring that very, very s pecial part of the world. I cannot stress enough the
cooperation, collaboration, and the desire for a very successful Anzac service,
2588 General Debate 25 Mar 2015
particularly this year, that will enjoin the cooperation and hard work from the Turkish
authorities, both central and local, and, of course, from our Australian friends.
I also had the pleasure this morning of laying a wreath with the Governor at the
Atatürk Memorial, which—if you do not know it —is at the southern end of the airport
on the right -hand side as you fly into Well ington. You can actually see it there. If you
do not mind, for the record, for Hansard, I really want to put the quote from Atatürk,
which just sums up better than anything or any words I have seen where we are today
with Anzac Day. The quote, which is the  inscription on the memorial at Gallipoli and
here in Wellington, reads: “ Those heroes who shed their blood and lost their lives , you
are now lying in the soil of a friendly country. Therefore rest in peace. There is no
difference between the Johnnies and the Mehmets to us where they lie side by side in
this country of ours. You, the mothers who sent their sons from far  away countries wipe
away your tears, your sons are now lying in our bosom s and are in peace. After having
lost their lives on this land they have become our sons as well.”
Those are prophetic words and also just humbling words. Every time I read them I
have a shiver down my spine. I have been quite humbled as I have been getting more
and more involved in my veterans’ affairs portfolio, which was given to me by the
Prime Minister late last year. There are good Kiwis, good people involved in our
services. They have been involved in our services, they still are, and they will be
involved in our services.
Many New Zealanders seem to somehow take for granted the sacrifice and the price
that many paid—and continue to pay—for the freedoms we enjoy to contest and to vote
in democratic elections and to enjoy our way throughout the world with our friends
throughout the world. I hope many Kiwis, particularly this year —some who, perhaps,
have not paid as much attention as they could as to who we are and what we are as a
nation—will perhaps take some time to reflect on this very, very special centenary and
commemoration. Thank you.

items.speaker: KELVIN DAVIS
items.text: This Government is a bit of a
shambles. It is stumbling from scandal to fiasco, and back to scandal again. Let me just
list a number of the fiascos and botch- ups that it has  made. It has botched up the
Northland by-election. The by-election, which is for an electorate that National has held
for decades and decades and decades, is slipping through its grasp as we speak. It has
absolutely mangled that. It has mangled the roads issue. It has mangled the bridges—the
“Simon Bridges” bridges. It has messed up that announcement. It has messed up
housing. What about this one: does anyone remember the cycleway —the cycleway that
was going to bring jobs to Northland by the thousand? It w as going to stretch from the
Bay of Islands across to Hokianga —80 kilometres of cycleway. Let me tell you now
that if you get on your bike and ride from Ōpua , you can ride 7 kilometres. Then you
have to get off your bike, you have to put it on the back of your truck, and you have to
drive about 30 kilometres to meet up with the next part of the cycleway. There are no
jobs that have been created.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: How long did that take?

items.speaker: KELVIN DAVIS
items.text: It has taken 7 years for a 7-kilometre long cycleway.
What else has it botched up? It has botched up Tim Groser’s job application for the
World Trade Organization. That is part of the scandal that this Government has been
involved in. And then there is the reason we are having the by-election in the first place.
This by-election should never have happened. I have always wondered why it is that
most ambitious policemen get a job in, say, Kaitāia , then they get promoted and go to
Whangarei, then they get promoted again and they go to a bigger station in Auckland,
and then maybe they get promoted again and they end up down the road here in
Wellington. Instead, Mike Sabin started in Whangarei and then his career went in
25 Mar 2015 General Debate 2589
reverse; he went from a big police station down to a small police station. And if the
National Party had done its due diligence, it would have seen that there were some
issues with Mr Sabin.
Then there comes the candidate selection. We have heard from Ron Mark over here
that National has gone and selected “Hoss Cartwright”—ju st give the man a stetson and
he would look like his twin brother. Not only does he look like Hoss Cartwright but
there has also been a bonanza in Northland. There has been a bonanza of bridges —10
double-laned bridges that we have not asked for. Those members would have had a bit
more credibility if they had just given us three bridges—but, no, they are treating us like
we are fools. They say: “Here are 10 bridges.” We are all asking: “Ten bridges? Wow,
that’s fantastic.” We are not going to look a gift hor se in the mouth, but their own
candidate cannot even name the 10 bridges. He could not even name the one that is a
hundred metres from his own home. It is not even going to take 5 seconds off the trip
from his front door, across the river to the Taipā  bakery—it is not going to take any
time off that. By the end we were thinking: “My gosh, after 1 week he’s making a $70
million, 10 -bridge announcement. Wow, this is fantastic! Imagine what he’s going to
announce after his second week—maybe an international airport in Te Kao, a stadium in
Hōreke, or a tunnel through the Mangamuka Gorge!”. Anything was possible with this
candidate. We even expected him to announce that the capital was going to be moved
back to Northland, where it started—but no.
What Northlanders actually want —if they had bothered to ask us —is stability of
roads. In the time of this National Government, $36 million has been taken from New
Zealand Transport Agency road funding. That is 29 percent of the funding gone. We
actually want stability of State Highway 1. If I get in my car at the start of Northland, at
Wellsford, and drive for about half an hour, I get to the Brynderwyns. The Brynderwyns
are windy on the south side and they have banks that slip down in adverse weather
conditions. On the north side they have long and straight curves with passing lanes. We
want the south side of the road through the Brynderwyns to be fixed. What does this
Government go and do? It has just started to fix the north side, which is not broken.
Then, if we are lucky enough to get over the Brynderwyns to Whangarei, there will be a
slip at Maromaku on State Highway 1. You now have to go through a little detour. If
you get past that detour, you get to Kawakawa. When it is raining and stormy,
Kawakawa gets flooded out, and you have to wait for a couple of hours to get over the
three bridges. If you get over them, you will get to Moerewa and the bottom of
Turntable Hill, and there will be another flood going on there. It does not matter which
road you take up to Kaitāia, whether it is State Highway 1 or State Highway 10. There
is the Kaeō bridge that gets flooded. There is the Waihou Valley bridge on State
Highway 1 that gets flooded. If you double -laned the Kaeō bridge, that would be great,
but it is not going to fix the 500 metres on the north side of that bridge that is flooded.

items.speaker: MATT DOOCEY
items.text: That member, Kelvin Davis, had 5
minutes to set out his vision, and he squandere d it. I learnt more from Steffan
Browning’s speech than I did from that member’s speech. Steffan Browning’s speech
was more coherent.
It does not seem that long ago that I attended the International Cricket Council
Cricket World Cup opening in Christchurch. There was a sense of excitement, there was
a sense of optimism, and there was a sense of hope. I would like to acknowledge the
fantastic win by the Black Caps over South Africa. Like many New Zealanders, I was
tucked up in bed last night enjoying a cup of tea and watching a fantastic game. I wish
the Black Caps all the best for their game on Sunday. Watching Grant Elliott hit the six
on the second to last ball reminded me of the cricket heroes that I grew up with: the big -
hitting Lance Cairns; the intern ational all-rounder Richard Hadlee; the talented Crowe
2590 General Debate 25 Mar 2015
brothers, Martin and Jeff; and the jovial wicketkeeper turned commentator Ian Smith. It
is great that the young people of New Zealand will now grow up with their own cricket
heroes.
We have our own regional development heroes in the Government: our team captain,
the Prime Minister; our all- rounder, Bill English; our fast bowler, Steven Joyce; and, a
pair of safe hands, our wicketkeeper, Gerry Brownlee. Not only have we seen the rise of
the Black Caps r ecently but we have seen the rise of another powerhouse: Canterbury
regional development. After the devastating earthquakes in 2010 and 2011, Canterbury
regional development is getting back on its feet. We saw the Hagley Oval—what a great
example of the first completed anchor project. Cantabrians are realising that not only are
we building a new city but our infrastructure and our facilities will be the best in New
Zealand, like the Hagley Oval. Coming up we have the bus interchange, the retail
precinct, th e Avon River precinct, the justice and emergency precinct, the health
precinct, the innovation precinct, and the performing arts precinct.
Recovery is not easy; it takes time. Earthquake recovery is a key focus of mine. We
are not just talking about bricks and mortar here. With a background in health—and,
specifically, mental health —we know international research tells us that years 3 to 5
post-disaster are the most problematic for social and psychological recovery. I would
like to remind people of the Canterbury District Health Board’s All Right? campaign. It
is worth repeating that if people are still needing help, it is all right to ask for help. I
would ask my parliamentary colleagues to ensure that we continue to focus on the
Canterbury earthquake recovery in 2015 and provide the support that Cantabrians need,
but the signs are encouraging. The 2014 Canterbury Earthquake Recovery Authority
well-being survey reported that 77 percent of Cantabrians rated their quality of life as
“good” or “very good”. These are the highest results for this survey in the last 4 years.
We do need to remind ourselves that it is not the Christchurch recovery; it is the
Canterbury recovery. In my electorate of Waimakariri, the town of Kaiapoi was hard hit
in the first earthqua ke in 2010. But this year, 2015, is the year of milestones and new
beginnings in the Canterbury earthquake recovery and in the recovery of the
Waimakariri. It has been an honour and a privilege to speak at the opening of the new
Ruataniwha Kaiapoi Civic Centre, the opening of the Rangiora Town Hall, and the
opening of the Ashley Bridge, and it was an honour and privilege to host the Prime
Minister for the reopening of the Oxford Town Hall. These community assets are not
only symbols of our recovery but of w here we are going in the future. I am proud to be
part of a Government that believes in community facilities for strong families and in
caring facilities.
We are looking forward to another great year ahead, and I am looking forward to an
open day for affordable housing in my electorate on Saturday, where affordable housing
is being provided for under $450,000. Many of my constituents are looking forward to
the KiwiSaver HomeStart loan package. Thank you.

items.speaker: Dr MEGAN WOODS
items.text: Well, what a show of “third- term-itis”
we have heard in this House today. Opening the batting today, we had the Hon Paula
Bennett, who was out for a duck trying to defend a failed housing policy that is lying in
tatters. But it was not just one duck because next up we had the “Minister of Bridges”,
Simon Bridges, playing a defensive game, caught on the back foot, and unable to make
any runs.
This is a Government that has run out of ideas. This is a Government tha t is playing
defence and a Government that is severely out of touch. We are seeing arrogance, we
are seeing bullying, and we are seeing a Government that is desperate to cling on to
power, whatever the cost and whatever it takes. Did we hear speeches today  from
25 Mar 2015 General Debate 2591
Ministers sketching out a brave new vision? No, we heard speeches trying to play patch
up, and speeches that did not work in trying to play patch up.
Then we had the last contribution, from new member Matthew Doocey across the
way. This was desperat ion at a new level. He had said in his office: “Oh, I know. It
might make us sound a bit better if I can compare us to the winning cricket team. That
might make it sound better.”, but that just did not work. It was desperation. He talked
about the rise of a new power. Well, given the state of this Government, we have to ask
whether that new power is Paula Bennett, Bill English, or Steven Joyce. Which one are
you backing?
This is a party where the wheels are coming off. National is about to do the
unthinkable—that is, snatch defeat from the jaws of victory —and possibly turn a 9,000
majority into a loss in Northland on Saturday. This is a Government that really is
playing off the back foot. We have got John Key’s increasingly bizarre outbursts, which
show that this is a Government losing control of its agenda and trying to protect its own
neck. This is a Government in disarray, as my colleagues have said. It is about scandal,
about botch-ups, and about fiasco. It is making a complete hash of things in Northland
and it is making some very, very strange statements in the House.
But there are some very serious issues that underlie this. We have been seeing for a
period of time now the abuses of power that this Government is willing to commit in
order to hold—and desperately hold—on to power. It is a Government that is riddled
with controversy and a string of these abuses. There is the smear machine that has been
run out of the Pr ime Minister’s office. The Prime Minister himself was shown to be on
late-night text terms with his bestie, Cameron Slater, on the eve of the release of the
Chisholm inquiry. We have a Government that is willing to use the resources of our
security intelligence agency for its own political ends —first of all, against Phil Goff in
the 2011 electoral campaign, and now we have the Government willing to use our
security intelligence agency as a recruitment agency for one of its Ministers. That is not
a sign of a  Government that deserves to be in power. That is not a sign of a group of
people who have a positive agenda for our country and want to implement it.
Then we have got the panic —the absolute panic—that is setting in over Northland. I
think the National Pa rty are in desperate need of a Corporal Jones within their midst —
someone to make the clarion call of “Don’t panic!”. Maybe it will be its whip Tim
Macindoe. He has just heard Matthew Doocey shop himself by saying that he goes
home early to watch the cricket rather than staying on until the end of play at 12, but it
might be his time to rise up and be the Corporal Jones and tell us “Don’t panic, don’t
panic!” because panic has set in on the benches opposite.
Whether Mark Osborne gets over the line or not on Saturday, National has already
lost in Northland. National has already shown that it is a Government on the way out. It
is a third -term Government that people are losing faith in quickly. The people of
Northland, like people all over New Zealand, are show ing that they are sick of being
taken for granted and of having their needs ignored, and they are going to punish
National at the ballot box. Whether that is a win or a close call, a close call is a loss for
National in Northland.

items.speaker: BRETT HUDSON
items.text: Well, New Zealand got off to a cracking start in
2015, just like the Black Caps last night against South Africa. We are wishing them the
very, very best for this Sunday, because I can tell you that for New Zealand Kiwis and
their families, under this Government, the success continues to roll on.
For the benefit of the aspiring Green Party leaders, I would like to point out that in
2014 the New Zealand economy grew 3.5 percent, one of the highest rates  in the
developed world. In the calendar year of 2014, inflation was merely 0.8 percent, which
was well below average weekly wage increases of 2.5 percent, and over the last 12
2592 General Debate 25 Mar 2015
months, 80,000 jobs were created and labour workforce participation rates reach ed a
record high. That tells us that businesses have confidence —confidence in what this
Government is doing, confidence in the future. They are looking to expand and to
employ more people. It tells us that the people of New Zealand have confidence. They
know that the work is out there and they know that they can improve their prosperity
and their livelihoods by seeking it. It all means more work, more income, and better
prosperity for Kiwi families. It is the heart and the start of better times for Kiwi
families.
This continues under this Government, with our Business Growth Agenda creating
more opportunities for Kiwis to succeed such as by opening new markets. This week we
signed a free -trade agreement with Korea. Korea is currently our sixth- largest expor t
market and contributes $4 billion to our economy each year, but under this free -trade
agreement we will remove $65 million in duty costs for Kiwi exporters in the first year
alone.

items.speaker: Todd Barclay
items.text: How much?

items.speaker: BRETT HUDSON
items.text: $65 million. That makes our exporters more competitive, and if
we are more competitive in Korea and other countries we are seeking to have free- trade
agreements with, that translates into more exports, more jobs, and higher incomes.
Along with this we are also  opening up channels of investment through things like
our Financial Markets Conduct Act, which passed recently and places a higher cap on
funding mechanisms such as crowdsourcing, which businesses such as Renaissance
Brewing and Invivo Wines have used ver y successfully. We are also making enormous
investments in quality and much-needed infrastructure.
Our roads of national significance are improving productivity and unlocking
economic potential throughout New Zealand. And we are seeing the benefits of that  in
Ōhāriu as well. We have got our own road of national significance. We are finally
seeing Transmission Gully under way and that is a much- needed infrastructure
investment in the Wellington region that will terminate in Ōhāriu . Along with that road,
we are also investigating a Pētone  to Grenada North link road, a road that could shave
as much as 7 kilometres off the trip from the north through to Pētone  and better link the
communities of Porirua and Tawa with Pētone. That is good, sensible investment.
Along with that investment, in Ōhāriu  we are also seeing a network of highly
successful and capable schools that are preparing our children for their brighter future
and contributing to the Minister of Education’s goal of five out  of five children having
success in education. It is a great news story. Ōhāriu  is the place to be. Everyone wants
to be there, and we are helping them with special housing areas, which we have agreed
with the Wellington City Council, in Johnsonville, whic h is the heart of the electorate,
and in Churton Park, a very popular suburb just to the north.
Our economy is flourishing along with Wellington’s. Wellington’s economy grew
4.4 percent in the year to March 2014, and Ōhāriu is playing its part. We have got beef
and sheep farmers in the valley, and they are now farming wind; we have got
technology companies that are hugely successful; and in traditional business, the Taylor
Preston meatworks contributes $250 million of exports to the local economy each year
and up to 700 jobs —much-needed jobs–in Wellington. It is a huge player in our local
market. Ōhāriu is playing its part and it is reaping rewards. This Government is focused
on the things that work with the things that will actually lift livelihoods and inc omes for
families. This Government is working for New Zealand.

items.speaker: PITA PARAONE
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Speaker. I just wonder whether I am in
the right place, because for the last 3 weeks all we have heard about from the other side
of the House was Northland and what National was going to do for Northland. And yet
here we are in the last week of a “buy -election” and all that those members can talk
25 Mar 2015 General Debate 2593
about is Anzac, and that is important; cricket, which is important too, but Ōhāriu ,
Korea, Johnsonville, Japan, Wellington, Korea —I am not saying that that is not
important, but, gosh, if I was a member of that party, I would certainly be wanting to do
my best for the people of Northland.
The Northland electora te is currently experiencing a political phenomenon that has
never ever been seen before in the last 10 years. The political party that Northland
people have pledged their faith in has deserted them, and what is National doing about
it? It talks about Northland being important and about what it is going to do for
Northland, but Northland is an example of regional New Zealand—forgotten. However,
that has all changed. Why has it changed? Because the “Force of the North” has arrived,
with a simple byline “Send them a message”. We are 3 days away from an election, but
the Government has already received the message, so that is very good. The people of
Northland are certainly taking the opportunity to send their message, and the reaction
from that side of the House certainly indicates that they have. It is great to note the
members who are present in the House. Obviously, they are the favoured few because
the rest of the team are all up in Northland getting ready to pull down the hoardings.
We know that the peopl e of Northland have been promised 10 two -laned bridges. I
am from the north and I am really sad. Although it may be good news for some people
in the north, I am really saddened that the bridge in Mōtatau , the bridge in Opahi, the
bridge in Pokapu, and the bridges at Matawaia, Pipiwai, Otiria —all within the Ngāti
Hine boundary—have not even been included on the Government’s list. Those people
who are living in those communities certainly do not believe that they have been
considered. However, once the New Zealand First candidate put his name into the hat,
all of a sudden the fruits, the baubles of office, started to fall down on Northland. That
is just an indication of the pulling power of our candidate, whom Northland people will
certainly provide their support for.
Talking about history, was it the National candidate who said that he would take the
Government back to Northland? Well, I just want to let you know that the New Zealand
First candidate has already beaten him to that. He has established his headquarters in
Russell, just down the road from Ōkiato , the original capital of New Zealand. So not
only is he preparing himself to represent the good people of Northland but also he is
indicating that there is a sense of history in all this, a history that will see tha t 70-odd
years of representation by one political party in this House for the people of Northland
will come to an end.
I have just one final thing to say. The Government had the opportunity to show how
sincere it was towards the people of Northland. In Northland there are 71 schools with a
decile rating of 1 to 3. Last week the Government had the opportunity of supporting two
bills that would see assistance given to families who were having difficulties feeding
their children. What did the Government choose to do? Ignore it —ignore it. And the
history of this country will show that all the filibustering that the National Government
has done towards helping Northland has been just that: filibustering. Kia ora.

items.speaker: JONO NAYLOR
items.text: I have got to say it is fantastic to be associated with a
Government that is assisting New Zealand families to get ahead. We are doing better,
and there is more on the plate that is coming. On 1 April we are going to see paid
parental leave increase by a further 2 weeks. This is great news for families. We are
going to see, again on 1 April, the parental tax credit for low -income families increase
from $150 to $220—more great news for families. The HomeStart scheme is going to
be up and running, and we are going to see more and more first -home buyers being able
to access the market. We are going to see free doctors visits extended, not just for those
who are under 6 but for those who are under 13 years of age. This is great news for New
2594 General Debate 25 Mar 2015
Zealand families. This is great news for our country as we build on our successes of the
past and continue to do more.
This is not a Government that has run out of steam. This is a Government that has
got energy. This is a Government that has got vision. This is a Government that wants
the very best for New Zealand families. Although we are making great progress in these
social areas in terms of the assistance we are directly providing to families, there is
more we can do and there is more we are g oing to do, particularly to empower families
to be able to provide for themselves, because that is ultimately the outcome we want to
see. We are going to do this by continuing to grow the economy. We are going to
continue to do this by growing jobs, and we  have got a good record in that over the last
little while. That is something that is happening right across New Zealand.
I hear constantly on the other side of the House people talking about a two- speed
economy where if you are not in Auckland or in Chri stchurch, then you are forgotten.
The regions of New Zealand have not been forgotten. The regions of  New Zealand, in
fact, are doing very, very well. We see the recent growth statistics that have come out
about regional development in New Zealand, and we see that things are going incredibly
well, things are growing at a greater rate, and we are in good shape.
If we are going to continue to grow the economy in the regions, it does take a little
bit of extra effort. Over recent times we have seen that extra effort go into regional
growth studies that have been occurring right across different parts of New Zealand —
particularly, so far, in the Bay of Plenty, in Northland, and also in the Manawatū–
Whanganui area, where I come from. These regional growth studies are working very
hard to identify particular areas that will be great opportunities for those particular
regions. I know that in Palmerston North and in the Manawatū, in particular, we know
we do some things better than pretty much anyone else in the count ry. We are
developing and working alongside this regional growth study to enhance those
opportunities further. We are seeing great expansion in the  area of food research and
development. With the help of the Government, through New Zealand Trade and
Enterprise in cooperation with local authorities, we are starting to see more jobs grow in
our region in this area. We have been able to attract overseas companies to come and set
up in the Manawatū, creating more jobs for locals. We are seeing New Zealand
companies like New Zealand Pharmaceuticals expanding their operations. They are
exporting more, and the region is going to do better, as well, because of it.
We are also the best place in New Zealand —the Manawatū—out of which to operate
logistics-type operations. The investment this Government is putting into the MacKays
to Peka Peka diversion around Waikanae and Paraparaumu is well on the way and is
going to increase the connectivity between the Manawatū and Wellington. Transmission
Gully is not too far away e ither. These particular roading projects are absolutely
connecting the region I live in to the capital city of Wellington. We know it is going to
have good pay-offs for us in this region and is something we will be very proud of.
Also, in terms of regiona l roading funding, the Foxton trestle bridge is due for an
upgrade. Unfortunately , at the moment it is unable to take high -productivity vehicles
along it, but when that bridge is done up, we are going to see high productivity from the
produce that is grown right around New Zealand getting better access to the markets.
I want to finish by reiterating that this is a Government that is going forward. This is
a Government that is very keen and committed to growing jobs, growing the economy,
and seeing better outcomes for New Zealand families.
The debate having concluded, the motion lapsed.

items.speaker: TIM MACINDOE
items.text: I seek leave for the debate on  the
bills that we are about to commence to be taken as one debate, with clauses to be voted
upon separately.

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Leave is sought for that purpose. Is
there any objection? There appears to be none.
Clauses 1 to 11

items.speaker: PHIL TWYFORD
items.text: I look forward to debating this bill
through the Committee stage, taken as one question. I want to begin by speaking to
clause 6 of the bill, which is the operative clause for what I think is the most significant
thing the bill sets out to do, which is to enable members of KiwiSaver schemes to
withdraw not only their own contributions but also the member tax credits, or the
Government contributions, in a KiwiSaver scheme in order to get a deposit together that
would enable them to take advantage of a Welco me Home Loan. This bill is an enabler
of the Government’s HomeStart subsidies, which were announced during last year’s
general election campaign.
We are going to focus our discussion this afternoon on the clauses in this bill, but let
me just note in pass ing that members on this side of the House —Labour members, in
particular—have been very critical of the policy for which this bill is an enabler. If I can
just summarise briefly our criticisms, we agree with many of the highly critical things
that have bee n said by the Reserve Bank, Treasury, and so on about the effect of
increasing homeownership subsidies in a market that is already supply -constrained,
where there is already significant excess demand compared with supply. Many
commentators, including the officials from the Ministry of Business, Innovation and
Employment, Treasury, the Reserve Bank, and the officials who briefed us in the select
committee, were clear that those were the problems associated with this bill.
Labour, as we have made clear in earlier debates, is going to be voting for this bill
because, putting aside for a second the HomeStart policy and the expansion of
homeowner subsidies, which we think will drive prices up and will actually make
housing more unaffordable, the bill itself is, at best, I suppose, slightly benign. But, as I
was saying, clause 6 is the one that basically amends the KiwiSaver scheme rules, and I
suppose the question in relation to clause 6 is, what difference is it going to make to
aspiring homeowners—to first -home buyers? Our calculations are that, at best, it will
allow possibly a couple of thousand, or maybe a few thousand, extra dollars to be
contributed to a deposit.
Put that in the context of what is happening, for example, in the Auckland housing
market, where over the last 12 months the average house price increased, on average, by
$1,700 every week—$1,700 every week. A bill that is going to enable people to add just
a few thousand dollars of their own retirement savings —so this bill gives people the
opportunity to raid their own kitty and, really, to pay the price of this Government’s
failure to address the housing crisis. But the quantum is all wrong. So, at best, it is going
to allow people to withdraw a few thousand dollars extra. It might be the equivalent of 2
weeks or 3 weeks of Auckland house price inflation, and I think that puts it in
perspective. That shows how incremental, how marginal, the benefit from this bill will
be.
I want to point to some of the comments that have been made by officials in relation
to the expansion of the subsidies, including the ability to withdraw one’s own retirement
savings in order to put a deposit together. Treasury advised the Government in July
2596 Taxation (KiwiSaver HomeStart and Remedial Matters) Bill 25 Mar 2015
2013 about the earlier change to the rules around eligibility for the Kiw iSaver home
deposit scheme. Treasury said that “The KiwiSaver Home Deposit Scheme increases the
cash available to homebuyers for deposits. Increasing eligibility may encourage buyers
to take on more debt/seek more expensive houses. This could exacerbate house price
pressures.” That is what we are talking about here.
Later that month Treasury advised that increasing KiwiSaver withdrawal subsidies
would have an impact on the very same financial and macro -stability issues that the
Reserve Bank Governor commen ts on on almost a weekly basis. Treasury said that the
impact on financial stability would be negative, and that it would undermine the
effectiveness of loan -to-value ratio lending restrictions, which is the main tool that the
Reserve Bank has brought in t o try to reduce the financial stability risks of an out -of-
control Auckland housing market. Treasury said: “Government subsidies for home
ownership are low value for money and tend to be regressive.” This is advice that
Treasury has given elsewhere. They are low value for money and they tend to be
regressive. So by raising the price caps and increasing the subsidies and the eligibility,
the Government is actually reducing the targeting and the value of the policy to make a
difference to the people who need it most, and it is expanding the pool of people who
are likely to take it up.
On the draft Cabinet paper —again, on the previous changes, but I think they are just
as apposite for this bill—Treasury said: “Experience with homeowner grants in
Australia suggests that such programmes tend to push prices up in a supply constrained
environment by supporting greater demand, rather than improving affordability.”, and
there is a risk that by expanding eligibility —as this bill does, and as the wider policy
does—for the KiwiSaver deposit subsidy, the Government will end up undermining
affordability for first-home buyers.
So I think that is a pretty good summary of the official advice about the implications
of clause 6, which allows the member tax credit, or the Gover nment contribution, to be
withdrawn. I think it is pretty clear that the benefit here is very, very small compared
with what is happening to house prices, which are up by 1,700 bucks a week in
Auckland. But the median house price for the whole of New Zeala nd has been going up
over the last 12 months by $1,000 a week on average —$1,000 a week. So the benefit of
this bill for aspiring first -home buyers is pretty marginal and is probably the equivalent
of about 2 or 3 weeks of house price inflation. Thank you.

items.speaker: RICHARD PROSSER
items.text: I rise to take a brief call on behalf of New
Zealand First and on behalf of my colleague Fletcher Tabuteau as we debate in the
Committee of the whole House the Taxati on (KiwiSaver HomeStart and Remedial
Matters) Bill.
As we have outlined previously New Zealand First does support this bill, albeit with
some minor reservations. I want to focus on one part of the bill that we do not believe
has received as much attention  as it warrants in terms of its importance to a very
specific and very important sector of society —that is, our returned service people, our
veterans. I am talking about clauses 8 to 11. We have a concern that this bill —rather
than being remedial as it is intended to be, and correcting certain anomalies —as it is
constructed will have the effect of compromising the potential income of some veterans.
This would be our single greatest concern, and I am sure the Minister in the chair, the
Hon Anne Tolley, will take the opportunity to rise, as she is wont to do, in order to allay
this concern, because we are certain it is not the intention of the Government to in any
way compromise the financial position that our veterans may find themselves in.
We understand that the intent of the bill is remedial with regard to veterans’ support
payments, that it is intended to tidy up parts of the Income Tax Act 2007 so that income
replacement payments under the Veterans’ Support Act 2014 are treated the same way
25 Mar 2015 Taxation (KiwiSaver HomeStart and Remedial Matters) Bill 2597
for tax purposes as are payments provided by ACC, and that they are taken into account
as regards social policy calculations, so that they do not trigger the application of rules
relating to auto-enrolment and the compulsory employment contributions to KiwiSaver.
This is admirable, and it is only proper and right, and we wholeheartedly support that.
However, we do hold a concern, as my colleague outlined earlier in this debate, that it
may in fact have the opposite effect under certain circumstances, and we would very
much appreciate the Minister taking time to address this.
The Veterans’ Support Act 2014 was legislation that adopted most of the
recommendations of the 2010 Law Commission review of the War Pensions Act 1954.
The commission made 170 recommendations and the Government adopted 132 of them,
which is admirable, we believe. The Act required reviewing because it was outdated. It
was designed to deal with the physical risks and effects of deployments, but it did not
cover the psychological or environmental risks a nd ongoing repercussions faced by
veterans—by service people who would become veterans. It focused on disability
compensation but did not provide for rehabilitation.
So the 2014 Act sought to address these anomalies, but, as is all too often the case,
the law of unintended consequences saw it falling foul of some unforeseen traps in other
pieces of legislation, notably tax law, which is what we are dealing with in this bill.
New Zealand First’s concern, then, is around the benevolent margin, and it is this  I
would very much like the Minister to provide some further assurances on.
The War Pensions Act was a form of workplace injury compensation in the days
before ACC, and some veterans qualify for compensation payments under the both that
Act and ACC while others qualify only under the older scheme. The RSA submission to
the select committee stated: “The benevolent margins for veterans, which so obviously
was a part of parliamentary thinking when ACC was established, has not in fact been
delivered as intended. Sometimes the letter of the law does not always manage to quite
capture the spirit of its intention.” I very much hope the Minister will undertake to
ensure, either by way of amendment or directive, to clarify the position of that intent.
The 2014 Act provided that “Veterans who are under the age of retirement and
unable to work because of any medical condition are able to receive a higher rate of
income compensation than is available under the 1954 Act, and surviving spouses or
partners, children and dependents continue to receive the same types of compensation as
under the 1954 Act.” We very much want to be reassured that the higher rate of
compensation provided for under the 2014 Act is able to survive the changes to tax law
brought about by this and preceding Acts, because if there is one group of people in
society who deserve the best deal possible it is our veterans, to whom we all owe a
collective debt of honour.
In closing I reiterate that New Zealand First will continue to support this bill. I look
forward to the Minister’s very erudite contribution, which we hope will be reassuring as
well.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: There are two important matters in this
bill, and in my  first call I guess I will look at the area I have a particular responsibility
for, which is veterans’ support payments. I think there are a number of questions that
the Committee needs to know about and actually the country needs to know about. It
seems t o me that the changes that are being made in this bill to veterans’ support
payments are way under the radar. I rang the RSA this afternoon just to see what its
view was. It did not know about the changes being made in this legislation. The chief
executive officer of the RSA did not know about this, and until I saw this bill I was not
aware of it.
On the surface this bill dramatically decreases the income of veterans through their
lump-sum payment, through their weekly compensation payment, and through the ir
2598 Taxation (KiwiSaver HomeStart and Remedial Matters) Bill 25 Mar 2015
weekly payment to the dependent spouse of a deceased veteran and to children and
dependants. It dramatically reduces their income because it makes it taxable.
I had to really look through the regulatory impact statement to find out what was
happening here. I read the Minister’s statement from the first reading, and the Minister
who spoke at the second reading did not even refer to it, but it appears that there has
been a massive cock-up. That cock-up is the fact that the Government did not get it right
in the first place. A veteran reading the Veterans’ Support Act would believe that the
income they were going to get was going to be non- taxable, and suddenly they find that
their income will go down by a third from what the Act apparently gave them, and,
what is more, it increases the obligations facing veterans in terms of student loans and
child support obligations. It reduces veterans’ Working for Families entitlements.
This has been conveniently swept under the carpet, and the excuse given is: “We got
it wrong. We made an error in the original Act.” This is an error, such that if any
veteran picked up the Act and looked at it, they would believe they were entitled to far
more than they are going to get as a consequence of this remedial piece of legislation.
My questions to the Minister are straightforward, but I would really like to get some
answers to them. That is the whole point of the Committee of the whole House stage.
My first question, Minister, is this. How did the Government make this stuff-up? How is
it that it got it wrong in the Veterans’ Support Act? What went wrong, why did it go
wrong, and why did it take so long to discover that? My second question is this. What
efforts have been made to communicate this error to veterans and their famil ies? Have
any efforts been made? It seems to me that people will have been misled by the
legislation originally advanced by the Government—the Veterans’ Support Act.
Thirdly, I take it from the regulatory impact statement, but I am not sure, that
payments have already been made to veterans. I would really like the officials to advise
the Minister as to whether any payments at the wrong level have been made to veterans.
If those payments have wrongly been made, to how many veterans were they made to
and what was the sum of money involved? Is this legislation retrospective? Will people
who have been getting more in payments than the Government now says they are
entitled to have to repay that money?
None of these questions has been addressed in any of the mat erial I have seen
advanced. I am hoping that the payments have not started and that there will not be any
requirement to pay money back. I will understand if the Department of Inland Revenue
made a genuine error but I think that when you make an error you front up, you admit it,
you explain how you made it, and you apologise for making it. I want to know from the
Minister whether any of those things have happened.
I had to, as an experienced legislator, search through the information that has been
provided by the Government, from every source, to find out that that was actually the
reason. It was swept under the carpet. The Government did not want to acknowledge it
and it did not want to admit it. When the RSA says to me that it did not know about it, I
think there is something fundamentally wrong with how our system is working.
I think they are fair questions, Minister, and I hope that you will take the opportunity
before this debate proceeds much further to get up and answer those questions so they
can be  clarified. Depending on the answers you give, of course, we may have some
further questions to ask.
The second area I want to speak on is the HomeStart -related clauses, clauses 3 to 6. I
am asking these questions on behalf of my constituents because I wa nt to know how
much these changes are going to help people in my electorate. My electorate is Mt
Roskill; it is on the Auckland isthmus. It is the area in which I grew up, and it used to be
an area where people could come and buy their first home. It was a  working-class area.
25 Mar 2015 Taxation (KiwiSaver HomeStart and Remedial Matters) Bill 2599
People could aspire, in the old days, to homeownership, they could have it, and it would
be affordable.
The really frightening thing, as I went around my electorate last year and knocked on
doors—doors that I had knocked on before; that I had known always, for the last 40
years, to be owner -occupied—was I found that they are now investor -owned and they
are being rented out. They are being rented out. Homeownership has gone from nearly
75 percent in my electorate, and in Auckland, to 61 percent. That is a serious, serious
indictment on what is happening in housing, because we all believe in the Kiwi dream
of being able to buy your own home. I am asking these questions because I want to
know whether what is in this bill will address that problem of housing affordability.
I would love my kids to be able to buy on the isthmus of Auckland. They cannot.
They cannot afford it. When I bought a home —and probably when you bought your
home, Mr Chairman—it was three times my income. That was the cost of my first home
as a first-home buyer. My kids are now paying six or seven times that income and they
have to rely on help from the family to be able to raise the deposit.
When I look at what is happening in Auckland with prices, I see the prices are going
up by $1,700 a week. Put yourself in the position of being a first -home buyer. You are
paying out high rent because of a housing shortage, and you have got to find $1,700 a
week more just to keep up with house prices. You cannot do it. Actually, a lot of
Auckland house prices have gone up by $90,000 in the last year—$90,000.
What do we do in this bill? We alter HomeStart so that we can give people their tax
credits back. It is $500 a year. That is what this bill provides to a first -home buyer—
$500 a year—and house prices are going up by $90,000 a year. So I ask whether this is
a genuine effort by the Government to address the problem of more and more people in
Auckland not being able to afford to buy a home of their own. Five hundred dollars a
year—

items.speaker: Carmel Sepuloni
items.text: It’s pathetic.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: Yes, yes —it is $10 a week, and house prices are going up by
$1,700 a week.
So I say that this is a drop in the bucket as an answer to a serious problem. But I say
more than that. When I read Treasury’s submission on what the Government is
proposing, it said that this will be counter -productive. It said that in a supply
constrained environment, putting more money in in this way is like putting petrol on a
fire to put it out and that all this will do —and it quotes the Australian examples —is
further push up prices, and that the poor prospective homeowners, being promised that
they ar e going to get something out of this bill, will just find that homeownership is
further and further outside their reach.
The statistics do not lie—75 percent of Aucklanders owned their own homes back in
the mid -1980s; today, 61 percent do. What difference  will this bill make? This is
tokenism, is it not? It is tokenism at best. Yet everyone in this House would say that an
important part of our democracy and our community is that people should have the right
to own their own homes. Well, because of the hous ing shortage they are paying more
rent, and because of the housing shortage house prices are going up more and more.
Who benefits from house price increases? Not the first -home buyer s—they are the
victims. The property investor benefits. With at least 40 percent of the houses sold
going to property investors, they are making thousands of dollars a week on every
property they own. That would be OK if it were not for the fact that they are making it
out of the hide of the people who are desperate to get into a home of their own.
Is this House working for property investors and not working for first -home buyers?
Obviously it is. We are introducing something here that will not provide real assistance
to the first -home buyer. The first-home buyer is falling further and further behind and
2600 Taxation (KiwiSaver HomeStart and Remedial Matters) Bill 25 Mar 2015
the Minister of housing, or all three Ministers of housing, insults them by saying: “Here
is something that will help you.”, when it will not help. Things are getting worse.

items.speaker: JAN LOGI E
items.text: I rise to take a short call in the Committee stage of the
Taxation (KiwiSaver HomeStart and Remedial Matters) Bill. I also want to put a few
questions to the Minister in the chair, Jo Goodhew, specifically in relation to clauses 8
to 11 and the changes for veterans. I did say in the first reading of this bill that I was
slightly bewildered to have this legislation in front of the House after just last year,
when the House spent such a long time considering the Veterans’ Support Bill, which
was in  turn the result of a very extended Law Commission report on the need to
modernise our veterans’ s upport system. Parliament spent many, many hours on that
legislation.
I have to say that at the very least I am bewildered to be here less than a year later,  I
think, with a bill that talks about remedial matters and is in fact, from what I can read in
it, proposing quite significant changes to what have been described as mistakes in that
piece of work. It is, I say again, a disturbing trend that seems to be h appening in this
House, where we are fixing up mistakes in the legislation of this Government. I would
like to hear clarification about exactly what the in -the-hand impact of this change in
legislation will be for veterans.
I did sit through the Social Se rvices Committee meetings and I am concerned. After
all the care we took in that committee listening to veterans about the hardship they were
experiencing, particularly as we are coming up to —and I am not one to celebrate war —
the 100th anniversary of Gallipoli, I am concerned. There has been so much attention to
remembering the lessons of that war and giving honour to the tragic losses and the harm
done to people sent into those conflict zones by this House, and the fact that we could
potentially be passing  legislation that would reduce their incomes and the support
available to them under the title of “Remedial Matters” is deeply disturbing to me, and I
really do hope to have that issue positively clarified to us in the Committee tonight.
I would also like  to speak about this bill in terms of a measure that National cited
during the election campaign as one of its key responses to the housing crisis—the crisis
that nobody on that side of the House seems to acknowledge is a crisis. Clause 6 enables
people to access their tax credits in their own KiwiSaver account if they are eligible for
the HomeStart provision and have the ability to access their KiwiSaver savings. As has
already been mentioned, I think it amounts to about $521 a year, which, in the very,
very best -case scenario is around $5,000, if they are old enough and enrolled in the
scheme at its first inception in 2007. So we are not talking about very much money. We
are not talking about any new money at all, because it was money that the Government
had already contributed and put into people’s KiwiSaver schemes. So it is just enabling
people to access a little bit more, which also means they will have less in the hand at
retirement.
It is critical to recognise how big the housing crisis is in this co untry. I think the
average age of first-home purchasers in the 1970s was 25, from the best evidence that I
can get from the library. The most up- to-date information we have got tells us that the
average age is now 34 or 36, and I would suspect it is quite a bit higher in Auckland
because that is a national figure. I know I am very lucky, living in the wonderful Porirua
East, to have been able to buy a very cheap house, but I know that is not the reality in
most of New Zealand. In fact, the average house pri ce in Auckland is now over
$650,000. Can you imagine that? That is more than three times my house price and it
requires a significant deposit. If you need 20 percent in order to have a deposit on the
average house, it is over $120,000. When you think about  how expensive rents are in
Auckland—and in many other places in the country —and about what people have left
over and their ability to save for a deposit, it becomes clear that it is impossible.
25 Mar 2015 Taxation (KiwiSaver HomeStart and Remedial Matters) Bill 2601
I was speaking with some caregivers up in Auckland on Monday  night, and they
were talking about working full time, caring for their kids, and living in Auckland. They
found a place close to their work, but after they have paid their rent they have less than
$200 a week left to cover all the rest of their costs and care for their children. You are
not going to be able to save for a deposit —you are going to struggle to feed your kids
when that is the reality.
So $520, which you already have from the Government, is not going to enable you to
get anywhere near $120,000. I do not think that clause 6 lives up to the Government’s
election promise. To consider this measure an answer in terms of home affordability
and people’s ability to buy their first homes is a bit of a joke, but we are supporting this
bill because—and it  feels weird even saying this —we know that for some people,
somewhere in the country, that little bit of money might be just enough to put them over
the edge into being able to buy their first house. It would feel curmudgeonly to not
support that. But, in terms of integrity, in terms of this being a response to home
affordability, and in terms of this being a response to the housing crisis, then the answer
is no, it is not.
I cannot imagine that anyone in this country listening to any of this debate would
have a sense of gratitude to the Government, or even a sense of confidence in the
Government’s ability to respond to the real issues facing this country at this time. So we
offer our very provisional support, and look forward to hearing the Minister answering
the questions around veterans’ support, because that in fact may change our position on
this bill. Kia ora.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: This bill, the Taxation
(KiwiSaver HomeStart and Remedial Matters) Bill, is something that is—there will be a
lot of discussion around homeownership and—

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: Tell us about markets again, like last time.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: Yes, well, I will tell you about it. You might learn something
as well. That is for the member over there, who has no idea what it is actually like to run
a business or do anything like  that. The important part of this bill is around that tax
credit that homebuyers will be able to access now. As many speakers have said, it is a
small amount of money compared with the purchase price, but still, when you are
getting the deposit together, a ny bit of money is very valuable. That is the whole point
of the matter, and it is why people would be wanting to take advantage of this piece of
legislation.
The wider context of this is that the Opposition parties are basically saying here that
this is ineffective in addressing the homeownership issue. That is what the Opposition
parties will be pushing along. But members of the New Zealand public realise and
understand that the biggest cost they face in homeownership is actually interest rates —
the inter est rates on the property. I just want to remind New Zealanders of what the
Opposition policy would actually give you in interest rates, and that is 9 percent interest
rates—9 percent. National’s policy gives you 6 percent interest rates —6 percent against
9 percent for the biggest cost that you will have in purchasing a property. That is the
point that underlies all the arguments you will see from the left. Basically, those
members say that the homeownership issue can be dealt with by 50 members of this
Parliament making certain decisions and then dictating how the market will operate.
In the Labour case, it is definitely a case where it believes that it can just go out there
and wave a magic wand and build 30,000 houses overnight —30,000 houses that will
not exist, will not last, and will not deliver for New Zealanders. The Green Party, for
example, thinks that 30,000 houses will just pop out of the sky —that you do not
actually have to build them. The Greens think that they come from just talking in this
2602 Taxation (KiwiSaver HomeStart and Remedial Matters) Bill 25 Mar 2015
House, and they will sort of come about. The New Zealand First Party —I think that it
thinks that 30,000 houses—

items.speaker: Stuart Nash
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Chairperson. I do understand that this is
going to be a wide -ranging debate, etc., etc., but actually I do think that the member
talking about Labour’s policies, New Zealand First’s policies, and the Green Party’s
policies is probably a little wide, even in terms of a wide-ranging debate.

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Thank you. The member is quite
right; the debate is wide-ranging. We are looking at all clauses together as one. Speakers
so far have ranged across the gambit of those clauses—

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: Were you going to say “rambled”?

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: I was about to say something I
probably should not have—the member is quite right. So we will call David Bennett.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: Mr Chairman, I am giving the context of the arguments that are
made so that when New Zealanders are listening to this debate they will understand the
context of the arguments that have been made. So it is very relevant. I know Labour
policy is hard to talk about, but I have tried m y best to encapsulate what little policy it
has.
Looking at it from that perspective, New Zealanders have a choice over how you
deal with the homeownership issue. You can see that one side of the argument is that
the Government itself can dictate the solu tions, the Government itself can build those
houses, and the Government itself will provide all those solutions. That has never been
